source.title: On the Relationship Between Activation Outliers and Feature Death in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Elana Simon; Etowah Adams; James Y. Zou

record.tranche_reason: The study reports SAE feature recovery and semantic-quality results on real pretrained models, including a protein language model, rather than testing toy-model superposition directly.
record.gate_note: The study measures SAE feature death, activation-mean effects, and recovery extensively, but those outcomes do not directly test the listed versions. Rows below cover reported real-model SAE feature recovery relevant to V4. The synthetic MMCS result is not included because it evaluates constructed ground-truth features, not features recovered from an LLM. The study's dead-feature rates and gamma correlations are also not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool to study why SAE features die (activation outliers, γ) and to evaluate its fix, mean-centering. Its real-model feature results (ESM3 concept coverage, Monosemanticity Scores) compare its own preprocessing with a baseline SAE. They measure the method's performance, not whether real models contain recoverable sparse features. ESM3 and DINOv3 are also not LLMs. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that dimension-level activation outliers, summarised as γ=‖µ‖/‖σ‖, predetermine SAE feature death at initialization (ρ=0.89/0.82 across 454 layers). They find recovery is bottlenecked by slow bias learning, and that mean-centering eliminates outlier-induced death and improves feature quality. They add that low-rank activation variance causes residual death, which PCA whitening fixes.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines activation outliers, SAE feature death, mean-centering, and feature recovery; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported feature-recovery outcomes vary with dictionary size and mean-centering. The paper also reports that feature quality and death depend on model and layer, but those broader death results are outside the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: On ESM3, raw neurons score near zero on the Monosemanticity Score while SAE features score higher. The authors take this as confirming that SAEs perform real decomposition (Section 6.2, Figure S16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In protein language models, SAE features are more monosemantic than individual neurons (indirect evidence of distributed or superposed representation outside LLMs).

fits_no_version.finding: SAE feature recovery and the effective dictionary size depend strongly on activation geometry and preprocessing (mean offsets, low-rank variance). Up to 70–98% of features can be dead, which varies by model and layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How many features an SAE recovers depends on preprocessing choices tied to activation geometry, not only on the model's underlying features.

record.peer_reviewed: ICML 2026, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR 306)
record.problems: The claim-relevant real-model recovery evidence is concentrated on ESM3; the Monosemanticity Score comparison is reported partly as a qualitative distribution description, without uncertainty estimates in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant real-model feature-recovery rows were identified. The many reported dead-feature, gamma, centering, and low-rank results were left out because they measure SAE training failure modes rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Toy-model superposition geometry and the sparsity-dependent transition. The synthetic data here are generated sparse-linear inputs used to test SAE recovery, not superposition in trained toy networks.
Whether LLMs spread features across neurons or contain SAE-recoverable sparse features. LLMs appear only in the dead-feature analyses.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features. The study shows dictionary outcomes depend strongly on preprocessing, but does not measure stability or canonicity.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites superposition only as the motivation for SAEs. All real-model feature-quality results compare mean-centered SAEs with baseline SAEs on ESM3 and DINOv3, so they are performance results for the study's own method. The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular arrangement of overlapping directions.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity pressure or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

The study evaluates SAE feature recovery and semantic quality in selected real models, but does not measure how broadly individual features are distributed across neurons or establish this across LLMs generally.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether the model's superposed features are fundamentally one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: ESM3

rows.measure: Number of biological concepts captured by at least one SAE feature
rows.note: The authors state that the mean-centered 2048-feature SAE captured more concepts than the baseline 8192-feature SAE.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (mean-centered SAE) with a baseline SAE on ESM3, a protein model. This is method performance, not evidence on V4. The values (61 vs 100) are read correctly from Table 1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ESM3 SAE features, at layer 24 for the reported concept-coverage comparison and in the reported Monosemanticity Score evaluation
reader_labels.reason: The SAE features recover biological concepts and show higher reported semantic quality; the evidence supports recoverable features in this tested model setting (r1–r4).
